All of that work is committed: df68cf1, b009ed5, 7357431, 76b97cd, 23dcea3. Working tree is clean.

The prior session added a large batch of new tests and bug fixes but never ran them through canon-drift-checker or canon-exit-gate the way the original 7 specs were vetted. Run canon-drift-checker against each of the 7 specs in .claude/specs/ again, specifically scrutinizing whether the newly-added tests (see the "Real bugs found and fixed" and "Test/quality state" sections of the handoff doc) actually assert what their spec criteria require, not just that they pass.

Report findings before fixing anything — I want to review what it finds before you touch code.
I'll start by reading the session handoff doc to understand what was built and what needs scrutiny.

1	# Session Handoff — 2026-08-12 SDD/Spec-Drift Initiative
2	
3	This session ran a comprehensive spec-driven-development (SDD) initiative across the whole
4	workspace: build a semantic-model reference layer, draft formal `spec@1` documents via the real
5	`canon` plugin pipeline, validate current code against those specs, and fix what the validation
6	found. It ran long and built a lot of context — this doc is the handoff so a fresh session can
7	pick up without re-deriving any of it.
8	
9	## Starter prompt for the next session
10	
11	> Read `docs/superpowers/session-handoff-2026-08-12.md` for full context, then: (1) review the
12	> uncommitted changes with `git status`/`git diff` and commit them if they look right to you —
13	> commit message should summarize the bug fixes and test-coverage closure, not just say "SDD
14	> work"; (2) the CLI spec test-coverage gaps (see "What's still open" below) are the best next
15	> target if you want to keep closing gaps — SPEC-CLI-001a alone has ~15 uncovered criteria;
16	> (3) alternatively, run `canon-drift-checker` again against the newly-added tests from this
17	> session (nothing has adversarially re-verified them yet) if the priority is confidence over
18	> coverage. Ask me which before starting substantial work.
19	
20	## What was done, in order
21	
22	1. **Phase 1 — Semantic model.** `.claude/semantic-model/` (7 files + `INDEX.md`): one file per
23	   subsystem (pipeline, extractor, resolver, types, serialization, cli, binding), each grounded
24	   in real source with numbered invariants and known gaps. Load via `INDEX.md`'s routing table —
25	   never load all seven at once.
26	
27	2. **Phase 2 — Spec drafting.** All 7 capabilities now have gated `spec@1` documents in
28	   `.claude/specs/`, drafted through the *real* `canon` pipeline (`canon-drafter` →
29	   `canon-verifier` → `canon-auditor` → `canon-exit-gate`), not approximated:
30	   - `SPEC-PIPELINE-001.json`, `SPEC-EXTRACTOR-001.json`, `SPEC-RESOLVER-001.json`,
31	     `SPEC-TYPES-001.json`, `SPEC-SERIALIZATION-001.json`, `SPEC-BINDING-001.json`
32	   - `SPEC-CLI-001a/b/c/d.json` (split from one oversized draft: exit-codes / atomic writes /
33	     LSP framing / config loading) — **already committed** as `df68cf1`, unlike the rest of
34	     this session's changes.
35	
36	   Several specs took many gate rounds (pipeline hit 9) because the adversarial gate kept
37	   catching real precision errors — worth knowing if you see `revision_note`/`reasoning` fields
38	   in the JSON that read like a long story. That's the gate working as intended, not noise.
39	
40	3. **Phase 3 — Drift validation + fixes.** Ran `canon-drift-checker` against all 7 specs (via
41	   6 parallel agents; CLI's 4 sub-specs bundled into one). Findings were split into
42	   covered / uncovered / **drifted**. Every drifted (= code contradicts spec) finding was
43	   investigated and either fixed in code or fixed in the spec, never left ambiguous.
44	
45	4. **Gap-closing pass** (this was the last major chunk of work, after the user asked to
46	   "make all sets of improvements we can make to close the gaps extensively"). Went
47	   subsystem-by-subsystem adding the missing tests the drift pass identified, verifying each
48	   new test against a deliberately-broken version of the relevant code before trusting it.
49	
50	## Real bugs found and fixed this session (7 total)
51	
52	All have regression tests confirmed to fail against the pre-fix code and pass against the fix.
53	
54	1. **Watch mode was permanently one edit behind.** `WatchSession::update_file` bound
55	   `new_global` directly to `ArcSwap::rcu(...)`'s return value — but `rcu` returns the
56	   *pre-swap* value (`compare_and_swap` convention), not the closure's result. Every
57	   incremental update resolved against stale content. Fixed via `load_full()` after the swap.
58	   `crates/core/src/pipeline/watch.rs`.
59	2. **`watch --out`'s stats were always zero.** `WatchSession::snapshot()` used

commit 7357431d5c032618a66e5d60fc789dd06f07e440
Author: Gabe Castro <gabe@techworx.dev>
Date:   Wed Aug 12 22:31:38 2026 +0200

    fix: close spec-validation findings across the whole workspace
    
    Fixes 7 real bugs surfaced by validating live code against the new
    spec@1 documents:
    
    - watch mode resolved every incremental update against the file's
      PRE-edit content — ArcSwap::rcu's return value is the pre-swap
      value, not the closure's result (pipeline/watch.rs)
    - watch --out's stats block always reported zero components
    - relative --config paths broke when their parent directory wasn't
      the invocation cwd (node subprocess cwd changes, path didn't)
    - NAPI auto-vivification (initialize_session/extract_file_incremental/
      create_session) ran WatchSession construction outside
      panic_guard::contain_panic
    - extract --out was never actually atomic, only watch --out was
    - watch's keyboard-quit hardcoded exit 0 instead of the tracked
      exit code
    - LSP verbose mode wrote tracing output to stdout, corrupting the
      Content-Length-framed protocol channel
    
    Also aligns chain.rs's depth-exhaustion path with the documented
    give_up contract, closes the test-coverage gaps the spec-drift
    validation identified across every crate, and adds two testing
    discipline rules to CLAUDE.md (sibling-path parity, assert-content-
    not-presence) that the bug pattern above kept violating.
    
    Every fix has a regression test confirmed to fail against the
    pre-fix code and pass against the fix.

1	//! Structural substitution for user-defined generic type aliases.
2	//!
3	//! `type Assign<T, U> = Omit<T, keyof U> & U` declares type parameters `T`/`U`
4	//! that are opaque names until a call site supplies concrete arguments, e.g.
5	//! `Assign<HTMLProps<'div'>, SelectRootBaseProps<T>>`. Previously the resolver
6	//! looked up `Assign` by name and resolved its body directly — `T`/`U` were
7	//! never replaced with the caller's arguments, so `Omit<T, keyof U>` resolved
8	//! against literal type names `"T"`/`"U"` (unresolvable) instead of the real
9	//! types, and the whole component's props came back empty.
10	//!
11	//! This module walks the alias body's `CollectedType`/`CollectedTypeAlias` tree
12	//! and replaces every bare `Named` reference to a declared parameter with the
13	//! caller's argument, before normal resolution proceeds. Purely structural —

## All 22 findings fixed (AC-017 + the 21 from the follow-up review)

**PIPELINE** (5 items): AC-017's test now actually distinguishes canonical from non-canonical paths via a transitive dependent (confirmed fail→pass against the real bug); AC-016b and AC-010 strengthened to check content, not presence; added 4 new tests for AC-015/019/020/024 (atomic replace, deletion, uninitialized session, non-UTF8 content). AC-001 (gitignore matrix) deliberately deferred — flagged explicitly rather than rushed.

**EXTRACTOR** (5 items): AC-014 now checks the diagnostic names "Wrap"; AC-022/026 check Error severity; AC-024 now covers all 5 named shapes; AC-009 got two genuine end-to-end malformed-`Omit<>` tests (the old one only unit-tested `record_skip` in isolation); AC-021/027 now check `props_type_name` values, not just key survival.

**RESOLVER** (5 items, plus one extra bug): AC-2/2b/3/4/5/6 all strengthened to check exact severity/code/message. Along the way I found and fixed a **real, previously-undocumented bug**: ordinary diamond inheritance (`C extends A, B` where both extend `Base`) was falsely reported as a circular reference, because sibling `extends` branches shared one cycle-detection set. Fixed by cloning it per-branch (mirroring a pattern `alias.rs` already used elsewhere) — confirmed fail→pass, documented in `docs/edge-cases.md`.

**TYPES** (4 items): AC-013 now asserts full `Diagnostic` equality; AC-004D2 covers all 11 string tags instead of 5; added a nested-NaN round-trip test covering all 6 enumerated positions. AC-005 was a genuine **spec-wording defect** (its own proving test necessarily violates its own literal wording) — amended the spec with a `#[cfg(test)]` carve-out rather than touching correct code.

**BINDING** (2 items): AC-4 extracted a pure seam so the full 65,536-call uniqueness bound is tested deterministically (the old version couldn't safely do this against the shared global counter without risking flakiness). AC-9 now uses `Arc::ptr_eq` to prove the *same* `WatchSession` is reused, not silently reconstructed.

**CLI** (3 items): Added real `extract --out` integration tests — including a symlink-based test that's the only one that actually distinguishes atomic writes from a naive `fs::write` (my first attempt didn't, and I caught that by trying to break it deliberately). Added the 5 missing LSP framing tests (AC-005b/c/d/006/007) plus the full exact-16MiB dispatch test. Added the config-path injection-safety test — confirmed it genuinely fails against a naive string-concatenation implementation with a real `SyntaxError`.

231	    fn key_for(&self, path: &Utf8Path) -> Option<CacheKey> {

Deriving the component name from the file stem (rather than, say, always calling it "default") mirrors how bundlers and tools like Next.js/Storybook already treat anonymous default exports — the filename *is* the identity. Splitting on `is_alphanumeric()` rather than a hardcoded list of separators (`-`, `_`, `.`) makes the PascalCase conversion resilient to any file-naming convention a project might use, without needing to enumerate them all.

# Root-Cause Analysis: `edge-cases.md` Findings

Phase 0 of the edge-case remediation effort. Four parallel agents each took a candidate cluster from `edge-cases.md` and asked not "what's broken" (already catalogued) but "what's missing that let it happen" — reading the actual code at every cited site, not just trusting the audit's summary. Three of the four found their assigned cluster wasn't one mechanism, it was several; after splitting, **11 confirmed mechanism-level root causes** and **7 genuinely standalone findings** remain.

**The overall pattern:** this codebase has good conventions in places that got established once — a named constructor, a depth counter, a truncation helper, a documented precedence order — but nothing makes those conventions load-bearing. They're advisory, so a parallel or later code path silently diverges from them. The fix shape repeats across clusters: turn an advisory helper into the *only* callable constructor, or add the one missing signal channel a class of code was never given. Two clusters (panic containment, schema derivation) are genuinely new architectural decisions and get an ADR; the rest are internal refactors of an existing-but-unenforced pattern.

**Adversarially verified 2026-08-04:** every root-cause diagnosis in this document was independently re-checked against the actual current source by a second, skeptical pass (7 agents, defaulting to refute). All diagnoses held up — no fabricated citations, no stale line numbers. Two mechanisms as originally drafted were **unsound** (would not compile, or would not stop the misuse they targeted) and have been rewritten below; several others were underspecified in ways an implementer would trip on and have been corrected inline, marked **[corrected]**. Where a correction narrows scope or changes the fix shape, the original claim is noted so the reasoning is traceable.

## Mechanism clusters

### 1. Resolver give-up constructor discipline `[corrected]`

**Root cause (narrowed on verification):** the original claim — "6 of ~10 `Opaque` construction sites bypass the named constructor" — overstated the blast radius. Verification found only **3 sites genuinely silent**: `func.rs:61` (`MultiParamFunction`, zero diagnostic anywhere nearby), `chain.rs:40` (cycle-detected `ResolvedChain::default()`, zero diagnostic), `alias.rs:116` (`LiteralUnion`-as-props-base, zero diagnostic, unlike the parallel diagnosed path at `alias.rs:234-253`). The two other sites originally named as bypassing the pattern — `primitives.rs:181` and `template.rs:39` — actually already push a correctly-shaped `Diagnostic` immediately before constructing the `Opaque`; they just don't call `collected.rs`'s helper, which is a private `fn` and structurally can't be called from those files today anyway. That's a duplication/style gap, not a silent-failure bug — don't conflate it with the real 3.

**Mechanism (rewritten — the original was unsound):** the original proposal — make `ResolvedChain`'s bare/`Default` construction private, and restructure `PropType::Opaque { raw, reason }` into a tuple variant `Opaque(OpaqueDetail)` with the only public constructor being a diagnostic-emitting `give_up()` — does not work, for two independent reasons verified against the real code:

1. **Reverse-dependency violation.** `known.rs` owns roughly 7 of the real `PropType::Opaque` construction sites and is required by `CLAUDE.md`'s "no reverse dependencies" rule to never depend on `resolver::ResolveState`. A `give_up(state: &mut ResolveState, ...)` signature as the *only* public constructor can't be called from `known.rs` at all. This split is intentional and already tested (`test_known_opaque_result_emits_diagnostic`, `test_known_opaque_result_emits_diagnostic_at_chain_level`): `known.rs` constructs the bare value, the *caller* (`chain.rs`/`named.rs`) diagnoses it via `push_known_opaque_diagnostic` using context `known.rs` doesn't have. ### Proposed: 0006. Derive JSON Schema instead of hand-writing it

**Context:** `schema.rs`'s hand-written schema has already drifted from `ComponentEntry`/`ExtractionStats`/`Diagnostic`'s real fields, undetected because the only test checks JSON syntax validity, not field-set parity. ADR-0002 already established the precedent of hand-writing `Serialize` for the three recursive enums (`PropType`, `CollectedType`, `OpaqueReason`) to avoid a recursion-limit blowup.

**Decision:** Derive `schemars::JsonSchema` on the plain output structs, including `OpaqueReason` (verified non-recursive, already using an ordinary `derive` for `Serialize` — not one of the hand-written cases despite ADR-0002's text suggesting otherwise); hand-write matching `JsonSchema` impls only for `PropType` and `CollectedType`, the two enums that are actually recursive and actually hand-write `Serialize` today. `cmd_schema()` calls `schemars::schema_for!(ExtractionOutput)` instead of building a `json!()` literal by hand.

**Consequences:**
- A second hand-maintained trait impl per recursive enum whenever a variant is added — the same "compiler won't remind you" tradeoff ADR-0002 already accepted for `Serialize`, now doubled. Scoped to 2 enums (`PropType`, `CollectedType`), not 3.
- Every plain-struct field addition is schema-correct automatically; only the two recursive enums need manual attention going forward.
- New dependency (`schemars`) — if that's undesirable, the floor-level alternative is a CI test that serializes a real fixture and validates it against the hand-written schema, catching drift without adding a dependency.

**Package:** `@oxc-react-docgen/vite-plugin` (`/Users/gabe/Projects/oxc-react-codegen/packages/vite-plugin`)

### How it hooks into Vite (`src/index.ts:15-165`)

`oxcReactDocgen(options)` returns a single `Plugin` object (not `Plugin[]`) with a closure holding mutable state: `sessionId`, `root`, `command`, `resolvedSrcDirs`, `currentOutput` (the in-memory `ExtractionOutput`, seeded with a zero-value placeholder), and `initPromise`.

Hook sequence and responsibilities:
- **`configResolved(config)`** (`src/index.ts:70-74`) — captures `root`/`command`, resolves `srcDirs` to absolute paths (`root + '/' + dir` unless already absolute), and calls `napi.createSession(napiOptions())` synchronously to get `sessionId`. No try/catch here.
- **`buildStart()`** (`src/index.ts:77-84`) — build-mode-only cold extraction. Guards on `command !== 'build'` and returns early otherwise. Calls `coldExtract()` inside try/catch, logs on failure via `console.error`. Added later (commit `62ff336`) specifically because Vite never calls `configureServer` during `vite build`, so without this the virtual module always resolved to the empty placeholder in production builds.
- **`configureServer(server)`** (`src/index.ts:86-112`) — dev-mode cold extraction. Fires `coldExtract()` fire-and-forget (`.then()/.catch()` chain, deliberately not `await`ed since `configureServer` must return its teardown function synchronously — documented at `src/index.ts:90-93`). On success, sends an `oxc-react-docgen:ready` HMR event via `server.environments.client.hot.send`. Returns a teardown closure that calls `napi.closeSession(sessionId)` — added in commit `49b12c6` to fix a dev-server session leak (comment: "`buildEnd` isn't called in dev mode — this is the only reliable cleanup hook", `src/index.ts:108`).
- **`hotUpdate(opts)`** (`src/index.ts:114-150`) — per-file-change HMR hook. Reads `(this as any).environment`, bails if absent or `env.name !== 'client'` (skips SSR). Bails if `!isSrcFile(opts.file)`. Awaits `initPromise` if set (so incremental calls queue behind the in-flight cold extraction). Calls `napi.extractFileIncremental(file, sessionId, napiOptions())`, parses the JSON result (with a try/catch fallback that logs and sends an empty update on parse failure), merges `updatedComponents` into `currentOutput.components` by `displayName` key, and sends `oxc-react-docgen:update` over HMR. Explicitly returns `undefined` (not `[]`) so Vite/React Fast Refresh still processes the file — documented at `src/index.ts:148-149`.
- **`resolveId`/`load`** (`src/index.ts:152-159`) — implements a `virtual:oxc-react-docgen` module (`\0`-prefixed per Vite convention) that serializes `currentOutput` as `export default {...}`.
- **`buildEnd()`** (`src/index.ts:161-163`) — closes the NAPI session; this is the build-mode cleanup counterpart to `configureServer`'s teardown.

`isSrcFile(file)` (`src/index.ts:63-65`): `(file.endsWith('.tsx') || file.endsWith('.ts')) && resolvedSrcDirs.some(dir => file.startsWith(`${dir}/`))`.

### NAPI boundary contract (from `packages/napi/binding.d.ts`, `packages/napi/index.d.ts`, and the Rust-side semantic-model doc at `.claude/semantic-model/napi-binding.md`)

The plugin calls exactly 4 of the 5 NAPI entry points (never `extractAll`, which is the CLI's cold one-shot path):
- `createSession(options) -> number` — sync
- `initializeSession(sessionId, options) -> Promise<string>` (JSON of `ExtractionOutput`)
- `extractFileIncremental(filePath, sessionId, options) -> Promise<string>` (JSON of `IncrementalUpdate`)
- `closeSession(sessionId) -> void` — sync

Per the Rust-side doc, all five entry points are wrapped in `contain_panic` (ADR 0005) so a Rust panic can never crash the host Node process — it always surfaces as a rejected promise / thrown `napi::Error`. This means the plugin's `napi.*` calls *can* legitimately reject/throw for real reasons (bad `reactVersion`, malformed `extraPathsJson`/`knownTypeOverridesJson`, a genuine internal panic converted to an error) — not just theoretical concerns.

## Prioritized Gaps / Risks (grounded in source, with citations)

**P1 — Dev-server session-leak regression has zero test coverage**
`configureServer`'s returned teardown function (`src/index.ts:109-111`, `napi.closeSession(sessionId)`) exists specifically because of a real bug fixed in commit `49b12c6` ("session leak"). None of the 18 tests invoke the function that `configureServer` returns — test #6 (`configureServer` describe block, `plugin.test.ts:86-98`) only asserts `initializeSession` was called; it never captures or calls the returned teardown. A regression here (e.g., someone refactors `configureServer` and forgets to return the teardown, or breaks the closure over `sessionId`) would not be caught by the suite.

**P1 — `hotUpdate`'s malformed-JSON fallback path is untested**
`src/index.ts:130-136`: if `napi.extractFileIncremental` resolves to unparsable JSON, the code catches it, logs via `console.error`, and sends `oxc-react-docgen:update` with `updatedComponents: []` and `diagnostics: []` — a real fallback contract (clients should still receive *an* event rather than an unhandled rejection). No test mocks `extractFileIncremental` to return bad JSON and asserts this fallback fires. Same class of gap for `coldExtract`'s JSON.parse failure (`src/index.ts:54-60`, returns `false` and logs) — no test drives `initializeSession` to resolve with malformed JSON.

**P1 — `initPromise` gating (the queue/replay race-guard) is never actually exercised as a race**
`src/index.ts:126`, `if (initPromise) await initPromise` — this is the mechanism described in the archived spec (`docs/archive/10-PLUGIN-SPEC.md:168`, "If `configureServer` is called before `initializeSession` resolves ... the `hotUpdate` handler queues updates and replays them") as the fix for a real ordering hazard: a file-change event arriving while cold extraction is still in flight. Every current `hotUpdate` test calls `hotUpdate` directly without ever calling `configureServer` first, so `initPromise` is always `null` in every test (`plugin.test.ts:39-44` `beforeEach` only calls `configResolved`, never `configureServer`) — the `await initPromise` branch's actual blocking behavior (does a `hotUpdate` call really wait for a pending cold extraction rather than racing it?) is not verified anywhere.

**P2 — Uncaught/unguarded `napi.createSession` throw in `configResolved`**
`src/index.ts:73`, `sessionId = napi.createSession(napiOptions())` is unguarded by try/catch, unlike `buildStart`/`configureServer` which both wrap their NAPI calls. ## 5. Session ID stability

`createSession` is called in `configResolved`, before the dev server starts. The session ID is stable for the lifetime of the Vite process. On `buildEnd` (or server close) the session is released via `closeSession`.

If `configureServer` is called before `initializeSession` resolves (race between Vite startup and cold extraction), the `hotUpdate` handler queues updates and replays them once initialization completes. Implementation: a `Promise` ref that `hotUpdate` awaits before calling `extractFileIncremental`.

## 7. Decisions log

| Decision | Rationale |
| --- | --- |
| Single `Plugin`, not `Plugin[]` | No internal composition needed; simpler for consumers to compose |
| Vite `^7.0.0 \|\| ^8.0.0` | 7 is current stable; 8 ships Rolldown (March 2026) — no API surface we use changes |
| No `enforce: 'pre'` | OXC reads disk directly; no need to intercept Vite's transform pipeline |
| `return undefined` from `hotUpdate` | Returning `[]` suppresses React Fast Refresh for the changed file |
| `environment.hot.send()` not `server.ws.send()` | Vite 6+ environment API; `server.ws` is Vite 5 compat only |
| `\0virtual:` prefix | Vite convention for virtual modules — prevents transform pipeline interference |
| Phase 5b (Rolldown) dropped | Rolldown 1.x has no external native Rust plugin mechanism; all plugins must use JS |

# Rollup Watch-Mode Hook Semantics

## `buildEnd` Hook Behavior

The `buildEnd` hook fires **once per rebuild** in watch mode. According to the documentation:

> "Called when Rollup has finished bundling, but before `generate` or `write` is called"

The documentation describes build hooks as running "during the build phase, which is triggered by `rollup.rollup(inputOptions)`." In watch mode, each file change triggers a new build phase, meaning `buildEnd` executes after each rebuild completes.

## `closeWatcher` Hook Purpose

The `closeWatcher` hook serves a fundamentally different purpose. It fires when the watcher process itself is shutting down:

> "Notifies a plugin when the watcher process will close so that all open resources can be closed too."

Key distinction: `closeWatcher` is triggered once when exiting watch mode entirely, not per-rebuild.

## Timing Relationship

- **`buildEnd`**: Fires after each individual rebuild (multiple times in watch mode)
- **`closeWatcher`**: Fires once when terminating the watcher process

The documentation notes that `closeWatcher` "can be triggered at any time both during the build and the output generation phases," emphasizing its global cleanup purpose versus `buildEnd`'s per-rebuild role.

123	## LSP — new bug found and fixed 2026-08-12 via Phase 3+ spec-drift validation
124	
125	- **FIXED.** Under `-v`/`-vv` (verbose tracing), `tracing::error!` calls inside `lsp.rs` were written to **stdout** by the default `tracing_subscriber::fmt` writer — corrupting the LSP transport channel, which requires stdout to carry only well-formed `Content-Length`-framed messages. A real editor session with verbose logging enabled would see this ANSI-colored diagnostic text injected mid-stream, desyncing the client. **FIXED**: `init_tracing` now routes all tracing output through `.with_writer(std::io::stderr)` — global, not LSP-specific, since stderr is safe for every command. Tests: `crates/cli/tests/lsp_process.rs`'s `verbose_mode_never_writes_tracing_output_to_stdout` (confirmed to fail against the pre-fix code, capturing the exact leaked ANSI-colored error line), plus 3 new process-level tests (`oversized_content_length_exits_1_with_empty_stdout`, `headerless_frame_exits_1_with_empty_stdout`, `well_formed_initialize_gets_a_response_frame_with_hover_false`) driving the real binary's stdin/stdout instead of only its pure helper functions. | `cli/main.rs:205-216` |

Checked the actual `callisto-moon` source to make sure — the answer isn't just "precedent," it's capability:

The WASM extension only implements two subcommands: `status` and `plan-publish` (`crates/callisto-moon/src/extension.rs:141-185`) — read-only introspection, nothing else. There's no `publish`, `tag`, or changeset-apply path through it. And it can't fully do even that: a `gix-spike` feature flag exists specifically to test whether the WASM guest can read a real git repo via WASI filesystem preopens, with an explicit comment that it's "never enabled in the shipped wasm" — meaning the production WASM build doesn't have working git access at all yet, let alone the ability to push tags, open PRs, or call the crates.io/npm registry APIs.

So this isn't close: WASM is objectively the wrong tool for what a release pipeline needs to do. The `callisto.toml` comment I wrote earlier ("moon is installed as a toolchain dependency, not as callisto's host") slightly understates it — the WASM extension physically cannot version-bump, publish, or tag, because release automation needs unsandboxed git/npm/cargo/GitHub-API access that a WASM guest doesn't have. It exists as an optional convenience layer for surfacing `moon ext callisto status` output inside a moon-native workflow for local dev visibility — not as an alternative to the CLI for actual releases.

The native-binary path via `callisto-action`/`setup-callisto` isn't the one we picked because michi picked it — it's the only one capable of doing the job. Nothing to change; the current setup is correct.

Confirmed with certainty via callisto's own test suite (`crates/callisto-graph/src/config/resolve.rs` and `tests/*.rs`): `[[package]] match` values are **package names** (bare or `<ecosystem>/<name>`-prefixed, e.g. `"cargo/other"`, `"npm/foo"`), never directory paths. My `callisto.toml` used directory paths (`"crates/core"`, `"packages/napi"`, etc.) for all six `[[package]]` blocks — every one of them silently matched zero real packages. `PackageId::parse` splits `"crates/core"` on `/`, checks whether `"crates"` is a recognized ecosystem prefix (it isn't — only `cargo`/`npm`/`pypi`/`go`/`maven`/`nuget`/`deno`/`jsr` are), and falls back to treating the whole string as a literal bare name, which then can never equal a real package's name. This is a real, confirmed bug in what I delivered — michi's reference config has the identical mistake, which is presumably why it went unnoticed. Fixing it now.

1	# oxc-react-docgen
2	
3	React component prop extraction powered by [OXC](https://oxc.rs). Parses TypeScript natively in Rust — no TypeScript compiler program, no type-checking pass, no startup tax.
4	
5	> **Status:** Core extraction, NAPI bindings, Vite plugin, CLI, and `docgen.config.ts` loading are complete.
6	
7	## Why
8	
9	`react-docgen-typescript` spins up a full TypeScript `Program` to extract props. On a mid-size design system this takes seconds — enough to noticeably delay Storybook startup and make HMR feel sluggish. OXC parses each file in parallel with no type-checking pass, so cold extraction on a 15-component fixture set (shadcn, MUI, Chakra, Mantine, React Aria, Radix) takes **32ms**.
10	
11	The CLI can emit an RDT-compatible shape via `--format rdt` (see [MIGRATING.md](MIGRATING.md)). The Vite plugin and NAPI binding currently expose this tool's own canonical format only — not a drop-in RDT replacement at that layer yet.
12	
13	## Install
14	
15	`@oxc-react-docgen/napi`, `@oxc-react-docgen/vite-plugin`, and `@oxc-react-docgen/cli` are not yet published to npm — there are no per-platform prebuilt binaries to install today. Until a release ships:
16	
17	```bash
18	git clone https://github.com/orin-dx/oxc-react-docgen
19	cd oxc-react-docgen
20	pnpm install
21	pnpm --filter @oxc-react-docgen/napi run build:napi   # builds the native addon for your platform
22	pnpm --filter @oxc-react-docgen/vite-plugin build
23	```
24	
25	`pnpm run build:napi` (not a bare `cargo build`) matters: it invokes `napi build`, which places the compiled addon exactly where `packages/napi/index.js`'s generated loader expects it. This works as a monorepo-local dependency today; there are no published per-platform packages for it to fall back to yet. See [MIGRATING.md](MIGRATING.md) if you're moving off `react-docgen-typescript` and want to know exactly what's compatible today.

1	# Migrating from react-docgen-typescript
2	
3	`oxc-react-docgen` targets output-shape compatibility with `react-docgen-typescript` (RDT) via the CLI's `--format rdt` flag. The NAPI binding and Vite plugin currently only expose the tool's own canonical format (`kind`-tagged `PropType`, shown in the main README) — there's no RDT-shape option at that layer yet. This document covers what's compatible today, what's intentionally different, and what's a known gap rather than a design choice.
4	
5	**Should you switch today?** If your components use plain interfaces/type aliases, `forwardRef` (including wrapped in an `as` cast), `FC`, HOC wrapping, `Omit`/`Pick`, `VariantProps` (CVA/TV/PandaCSS), or discriminated unions (including ones wrapped in an intersection) — yes, output should match closely. If you scrape the full 250+ inherited HTML attributes per component, read the [HTML attribute inheritance](#html-attribute-inheritance) section below — it's supported, but opt-in.
6	
7	## Field-by-field comparison
8	
9	### Component level (`ComponentDoc`)
10	
11	| RDT field | `--format rdt` | Notes |
12	| --- | --- | --- |
13	| `displayName` | ✅ |  |
14	| `description` | ✅ | From the component's own leading JSDoc, if any |
15	| `props` | ✅ | See prop-level table below |
16	| `methods` | ✅ (always `[]`) | RDT only populates this for class components; we don't support class components, so it's always empty — present for shape compatibility, not because we detect methods |
17	| `tags` | ✅ | JSDoc `@tag` values on the component declaration (e.g. `@deprecated`, `@since`) — not part of RDT's original spec but included since some tooling reads it |
18	
19	### Prop level (`PropItem`)
20	
21	| RDT field | `--format rdt` | Notes |
22	| --- | --- | --- |
23	| `name` | ✅ |  |
24	| `required` | ✅ |  |
25	| `type.name` | ✅ | Literal unions emit `{name: "enum", value: [...]}` matching RDT's convention (so Storybook-style `<select>` controls activate) instead of inlining the literal text |
26	| `description` | ✅ |  |
27	| `defaultValue` | ✅ | `{value, computed}` — captured from destructured parameter defaults (`{ variant = 'primary' }`) or JSDoc `@default`, code value wins on conflict |
28	| `parent.name` / `parent.fileName` | ✅ | `fileName` is always canonicalized to an absolute path regardless of how `--src` was invoked |
29	| `declarations` | ❌ not emitted in `--format rdt` | Only present in `--format canonical` (the raw internal shape); omitted from both `--format rdt` and `--format storybook` to match RDT's single-parent shape. File an issue if you need it |
30	
31	### Intentionally omitted
32	
33	| Prop | Why |
34	| --- | --- |
35	| `ref` | Not a user-facing prop — a React internal. RDT includes it because it walks the full inherited type; we treat it as noise |
36	| `key` | Same reasoning as `ref` |
37	
38	### HTML attribute inheritance
39	
40	RDT inlines every inherited HTML attribute (e.g. all ~250-300 members of `ButtonHTMLAttributes`) directly into `props`. By default, we don't — but you can turn this on:
41	
42	- **Default (curated):** `inheritance` (canonical format only) records the layer itself (`ButtonHTMLAttributes`, the element it maps to, what was `Omit`-ted), and `notableInherited` surfaces ~15-20 curated, commonly-documented HTML attributes per element (`onClick`, `disabled`, `type`, ARIA attributes, etc.) rather than the full set. `--format rdt` does **not** include `notableInherited` at all in this mode — RDT consumers that filter by `parent.fileName.includes('node_modules')` to drop inherited noise will simply see fewer inherited props than RDT provides, not extra/wrong ones.

1	# Architecture
2	
3	## Pipeline
4	
5	Every extraction — cold or incremental — flows through four phases:
6	
7	```mermaid
8	flowchart LR
9	    src["Source files\n.ts / .tsx / .d.ts"]
10	    oxc["OXC parser\none allocator per file"]
11	    sd["SourceData\ninterfaces, type aliases,\nimport bindings, defaults"]
12	    gsd["GlobalSourceData\nmerged across all files\nArc<ArcSwap<…>>"]
13	    ce["ComponentEntry\nresolved props,\ninheritance chain"]
14	    out["ExtractionOutput\nJSON-serializable"]
15	
16	    src -->|"discover_files()\nignore crate"| oxc
17	    oxc -->|"parse_file()\nper-file parallel"| sd
18	    sd -->|"rayon par_iter\nmerge()"| gsd
19	    gsd -->|"resolve_component()\nper-component parallel"| ce
20	    ce -->|"pipeline::extract()"| out
21	```
22	
23	Each `parse_file()` call gets its own OXC allocator. No AST node escapes the function — all extracted data is owned, heap-allocated types. This is what makes the rayon parallelism safe.
24	
25	The watch path reuses `GlobalSourceData` across file changes. A single-file update calls `parse_file()` on the changed file, merges via `ArcSwap::rcu` (retries on concurrent write), then re-resolves only the affected components.

1	# oxc-react-docgen
2	
3	React component prop extraction powered by [OXC](https://oxc.rs). Parses TypeScript natively in Rust — no TypeScript compiler program, no type-checking pass, no startup tax.
4	
5	> **Status:** Core extraction, NAPI bindings, Vite plugin, CLI, and `docgen.config.ts` loading are complete.
6	
7	## Why
8	
9	`react-docgen-typescript` spins up a full TypeScript `Program` to extract props. On a mid-size design system that takes seconds — enough to noticeably delay Storybook startup and make HMR feel sluggish.
10	
11	OXC parses each file in parallel with no type-checking pass:
12	
13	- **Cold extraction, 21 real component libraries:** 50ms ([full breakdown](docs/benchmarks.md))
14	- **Incremental single-file update:** ~2ms — react-docgen-typescript has no equivalent API; every edit re-pays the full cold cost
15	
16	The CLI can emit an RDT-compatible shape via `--format rdt` (see [MIGRATING.md](MIGRATING.md)). The Vite plugin and NAPI binding currently expose this tool's own canonical format only — not a drop-in RDT replacement at that layer yet.
17	
18	## Install
19	
20	> Not yet on npm. No prebuilt per-platform binaries exist yet — build from source:
21	
22	```bash
23	git clone https://github.com/orin-dx/oxc-react-docgen
24	cd oxc-react-docgen
25	pnpm install
26	pnpm --filter @oxc-react-docgen/napi run build:napi   # builds the native addon for your platform
27	pnpm --filter @oxc-react-docgen/vite-plugin build
28	```
29	
30	Use `pnpm run build:napi`, not a bare `cargo build` — it invokes `napi build`, which places the compiled addon exactly where `packages/napi/index.js`'s loader expects it.
31	
32	Migrating off `react-docgen-typescript`? See [MIGRATING.md](MIGRATING.md) for what's compatible today.

1	# Migrating from react-docgen-typescript
2	
3	`oxc-react-docgen` targets output-shape compatibility with `react-docgen-typescript` (RDT) via the CLI's `--format rdt` flag. The NAPI binding and Vite plugin currently only expose this tool's own canonical format (`kind`-tagged `PropType`, shown in the main README) — no RDT-shape option at that layer yet.
4	
5	This document covers what's compatible today, what's intentionally different, and what's a known gap rather than a design choice.
6	
7	## Should you switch today?
8	
9	Output should match closely if your components use:
10	
11	- Plain interfaces or type aliases
12	- `forwardRef` (including wrapped in an `as` cast), `FC`, or HOC wrapping
13	- `Omit` / `Pick`
14	- `VariantProps` (CVA / TV / PandaCSS)
15	- Discriminated unions (including ones wrapped in an intersection)
16	
17	Scraping the full 250+ inherited HTML attributes per component? It's supported, but opt-in — see [HTML attribute inheritance](#html-attribute-inheritance) below.
18	
19	## Field-by-field comparison
20	
21	### Component level (`ComponentDoc`)
22	
23	| RDT field | `--format rdt` | Notes |
24	| --- | --- | --- |
25	| `displayName` | ✅ |  |
26	| `description` | ✅ | From the component's own leading JSDoc, if any |
27	| `props` | ✅ | See prop-level table below |
28	| `methods` | ✅ (always `[]`) | RDT only populates this for class components; we don't support class components, so it's always empty — present for shape compatibility, not because we detect methods |
29	| `tags` | ✅ | JSDoc `@tag` values on the component declaration (e.g. `@deprecated`, `@since`) — not part of RDT's original spec but included since some tooling reads it |
30	
31	### Prop level (`PropItem`)
32	
33	| RDT field | `--format rdt` | Notes |
34	| --- | --- | --- |
35	| `name` | ✅ |  |
36	| `required` | ✅ |  |
37	| `type.name` | ✅ | Literal unions emit `{name: "enum", value: [...]}` matching RDT's convention (so Storybook-style `<select>` controls activate) instead of inlining the literal text |
38	| `description` | ✅ |  |
39	| `defaultValue` | ✅ | `{value, computed}` — captured from destructured parameter defaults (`{ variant = 'primary' }`) or JSDoc `@default`, code value wins on conflict |
40	| `parent.name` / `parent.fileName` | ✅ | `fileName` is always canonicalized to an absolute path regardless of how `--src` was invoked |
41	| `declarations` | ❌ not emitted in `--format rdt` | Only present in `--format canonical` (the raw internal shape); omitted from both `--format rdt` and `--format storybook` to match RDT's single-parent shape. File an issue if you need it |
42	
43	### Intentionally omitted
44	
45	| Prop | Why |
46	| --- | --- |
47	| `ref` | Not a user-facing prop — a React internal. RDT includes it because it walks the full inherited type; we treat it as noise |
48	| `key` | Same reasoning as `ref` |
49	
50	### HTML attribute inheritance
51	
52	RDT inlines every inherited HTML attribute (e.g. all ~250-300 members of `ButtonHTMLAttributes`) directly into `props`. This tool doesn't, by default — set `--html-attributes` to control it:
53	
54	| Mode | Behavior | Reaches `--format rdt` |
55	| --- | --- | --- |
56	| `curated` (default) | ~15-20 commonly-documented attributes per element (`onClick`, `disabled`, `type`, ARIA attrs) in `notableInherited`. `inheritance` (canonical format only) still records the full layer — element, `Omit`-ted keys. | No |
57	| `full` | Resolves `@types/react`'s real `HTMLAttributes`/`AriaAttributes`/`DOMAttributes`/`<Element>HTMLAttributes` chain and merges it directly into `props`, matching RDT's flat behavior. | Yes |
58	| `none` | Own-declared props only. | Yes (nothing to add) |

24

26	| --- | --- |
27	| Generic parameter substitution (`List<T>` where T flows from call-site) | OXC gives us the AST node `T`, but to know T's concrete value we need the checker's `getTypeAtLocation` or its tsgo equivalent |

34	## TypeScript 7.0 / tsgo ecosystem status (as of 2026-06-28)
35	
36	### What happened
37	
38	TypeScript 7.0 RC shipped 2026-06-18. This is the Go rewrite of the compiler ("tsgo"), not a JavaScript refactor. The key changes:
39	
40	- **TypeScript 6.0** = last JavaScript-based tsc (maintenance only)
41	- **TypeScript 7.0** = Go rewrite; 10× build speed, same semantics
42	- **Strada API** (ts.createProgram, checker.getTypeAtLocation, LanguageService) = **completely dropped** in TS 7.0 — no shim, no compatibility layer
43	- **react-docgen-typescript** depends on Strada; it is **broken under TS 7.0**
44	
45	### Corsa API
46	
47	The tsgo team is building "Corsa" as the replacement public API. Status:
48	
49	- Corsa API: **not yet stable** — targeting TypeScript 7.1 (estimated late 2026 / early 2027)
50	- Current tsgo exports minimal surface: `check()`, `build()`, basic diagnostics
51	- No `getTypeAtLocation` equivalent yet
52	- Plugin system and language service extensions TBD
53	
54	### tsgolint precedent (OXC team)
55	
56	The OXC team already tackled cross-language integration with `tsgolint`:
57	
58	- Spawns `tsgo` as a subprocess
59	- Communicates via JSON IPC using tsgo's internal (unstable) shims
60	- This pattern works but depends on internal APIs that will break when Corsa lands
61	
62	We should NOT follow the tsgolint approach — it creates maintenance debt on an unstable internal API. Wait for Corsa.
63	
64	### Why oxc-react-docgen is unaffected by TS 7.0
65	
66	We parse TypeScript with OXC (Rust), not tsc. We have no dependency on the Strada API. Consumers running TS 7.0 can use oxc-react-docgen without any changes. This is a competitive advantage during the TS 6→7 migration window.

1	# oxc-react-docgen
2	
3	React component prop extraction powered by [OXC](https://oxc.rs). Parses TypeScript natively in Rust — no TypeScript compiler program, no type-checking pass, no startup tax.
4	
5	> **Status:** Core extraction, NAPI bindings, Vite plugin, CLI, and `docgen.config.ts` loading are complete.
6	
7	## Why
8	
9	`react-docgen-typescript` spins up a full TypeScript `Program` to extract props. On a mid-size design system that takes seconds — enough to noticeably delay Storybook startup and make HMR feel sluggish.
10	
11	OXC parses each file in parallel with no type-checking pass:
12	
13	- **Cold extraction, 21 real component libraries:** 50ms ([full breakdown](docs/benchmarks.md))
14	- **Incremental single-file update:** ~2ms — react-docgen-typescript has no equivalent API; every edit re-pays the full cold cost
15	
16	The CLI can emit an RDT-compatible shape via `--format rdt` (see [MIGRATING.md](MIGRATING.md)). The Vite plugin and NAPI binding currently expose this tool's own canonical format only — not a drop-in RDT replacement at that layer yet.
17	
18	## Install
19	
20	> Not yet on npm. No prebuilt per-platform binaries exist yet — build from source:
21	
22	```bash
23	git clone https://github.com/orin-dx/oxc-react-docgen
24	cd oxc-react-docgen
25	pnpm install
26	pnpm --filter @oxc-react-docgen/napi run build:napi   # builds the native addon for your platform
27	pnpm --filter @oxc-react-docgen/vite-plugin build
28	```
29	
30	Use `pnpm run build:napi`, not a bare `cargo build` — it invokes `napi build`, which places the compiled addon exactly where `packages/napi/index.js`'s loader expects it.
31	
32	Migrating off `react-docgen-typescript`? See [MIGRATING.md](MIGRATING.md) for what's compatible today.
33	
34	## Vite plugin
35	
36	```ts
37	// vite.config.ts
38	import { defineConfig } from 'vite'
39	import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react'
40	import { oxcReactDocgen } from '@oxc-react-docgen/vite-plugin'
41	
42	export default defineConfig({
43	  plugins: [react(), oxcReactDocgen({ srcDirs: ['src'] })],
44	})
45	```
46	
47	Metadata is available on the `virtual:oxc-react-docgen` module and pushed via HMR as components change:
48	
49	```ts
50	import docgen from 'virtual:oxc-react-docgen'
51	
52	docgen.components['Button'].props
53	// {
54	//   variant: {
55	//     type: { kind: 'literalUnion', members: ['default', 'destructive', 'outline'], hasDefault: true },
56	//     required: false,
57	//     defaultValue: { value: '"default"', computed: false },
58	//     description: '',
59	//   },
60	//   ...
61	// }
62	```
63	
64	## CLI
65	
66	A single Rust binary (`crates/cli`) — argument parsing, output formatting, and `--format rdt`/`--format storybook` serialization all live there. `@oxc-react-docgen/cli` (once published) is a thin npm wrapper that execs the platform-appropriate compiled binary — no reimplemented logic, so there's exactly one place CLI behavior can drift.
67	
68	```bash
69	# Once published: npx @oxc-react-docgen/cli extract --src src/ --out docgen.json
70	# From source today: ./target/release/oxc-react-docgen (after cargo build --release)
71	
72	# One-shot extraction
73	oxc-react-docgen extract --src src/ --out docgen.json
74	
75	# Inspect a single file
76	oxc-react-docgen inspect src/components/Button.tsx
77	
78	# Watch mode
79	oxc-react-docgen watch --src src/
80	
81	# Shell completions
82	oxc-react-docgen completions zsh > ~/.zsh/completions/_oxc-react-docgen
83	
84	# Full HTML attribute expansion instead of the default curated subset
85	oxc-react-docgen extract --src src/ --html-attributes full
86	```
87	
88	Settings can also live in `docgen.config.ts` (`srcDirs`, `htmlAttributes`, `reactVersion`, `crossPackage`, and more — see `crates/cli/src/config.rs` for the full schema) instead of CLI flags.

Investigate whether this repo has a Cargo-workspace build-lock serialization bug in its
CI/lint/test task runner (moon, Turborepo, Nx, Makefile, or similar), and fix it if so.

## Background

Cargo takes a process-level file lock on a workspace's shared `target/` directory for the
duration of any `cargo` invocation (build, check, clippy, test) touching it. If a monorepo
task runner fans out one `cargo <cmd> -p $crate` invocation per crate — even when it *thinks*
it's running them in parallel — every one of those processes contends for the same lock, so
they serialize behind each other. The task runner's own parallelism is real at the process-
spawn level; Cargo silently defeats it underneath. Symptom: a lint/build/test step that "hangs"
or takes 10-60+ minutes even though no single crate should take that long, with repeated
"Blocking waiting for file lock on build directory" lines in verbose output — easy to
misdiagnose as a hung process, a bad dependency (heavy C-linked crates like aws-lc-sys/ring/
wasmtime are common red herrings), or a caching bug, when it's actually just N processes
queued behind one lock.

This is a known, acknowledged Cargo/monorepo-tool interaction — moonrepo's own Rust handbook
states it explicitly: "if you do per-crate, Cargo itself will 'wait for build lock' when
multiple processes are running," and recommends workspace-wide invocations instead.

## Diagnose

1. Find the task definition that runs clippy/build/test per-crate (e.g. a global task template
   with `-p $project` or equivalent, applied to every package).
2. Run the full task with verbose/streaming output and check for repeated
   "Blocking waiting for file lock" lines, and whether wall-clock time is roughly the *sum* of
   each crate's individual build time rather than the *max*.
3. Confirm: kill everything, run one crate's task alone and time it, then run the full fan-out
   and compare total wall time against (that time) × (crate count). If they're close, this is
   the bug.

## Fix

Two changes, not one — they serve different call sites:

1. **Full-scope runs (CI, `just ci`-equivalent):** replace the per-crate fan-out with a single
   `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` (same pattern for `build`/`test`,
   though `cargo test --workspace` doesn't run doctests — pair with `cargo test --doc`, or use
   `cargo nextest run --workspace` and fall back to the runner's own task for coverage it
   doesn't handle). One process, Cargo's internal job scheduler parallelizes compilation across
   crates on its own — no lock contention because there's only one lock-holder.

2. **Affected-only runs (pre-push, incremental CI):** don't drop the task runner's affected-
   project detection — it's real, dependency-graph-aware signal a plain Cargo invocation can't
   compute on its own. Instead of letting it *execute* per-project (which reintroduces the same
   lock problem at a smaller scale whenever 2+ projects are affected), use it only to *build the
   scope*, then feed that into one Cargo invocation with multiple `-p` flags:
   projects=$(<task-runner query for affected project ids>)
   if [ -z "$projects" ]; then exit 0; fi
   args=(); for p in $projects; do args+=(-p "$p"); done
   cargo clippy "${args[@]}" --all-targets -- -D warnings
For moon specifically: `moon query projects --affected` returns JSON with a `.projects[].id`
array of exactly the changed crates (verified: touching two crates' files returns exactly
those two project ids, nothing else) — pipe that through `jq -r '.projects[].id'`.

Do not scope lint to affected crates' *downstream dependents* — clippy warnings are about a
crate's own source, not its callers, so only the changed crates themselves need relinting. Test
scoping is a separate, judgment-call question (a changed crate's behavior can break a
downstream crate's integration tests) — don't fold that into a lint fix without deciding it
explicitly.

## Verify

- Time the old fan-out path once for a real before/after number, not just "it feels faster."
- Test both the zero-affected case (clean tree → instant no-op) and a multi-affected case
  (touch 2+ unrelated crates → confirm the resulting single command lints exactly those crates
  and nothing else) before trusting the fix.
- Re-run the repo's full CI/lint suite once after the change to confirm nothing else broke.

**Confirmed: real bug, now fixed.**

**Diagnosis:** `moon run :build`/`:test`/`:lint` (used by `justfile`'s `build` recipe and root `package.json`'s `build`/`test`/`lint` scripts) fan out per-crate `cargo build/clippy/nextest -p <crate>` across `crates/core`, `crates/cli`, `crates/binding` — each a separate process contending for the same `target/` lock. Reproduced live: a clean `moon run :build` showed `cli:build` and `crates-binding:build` racing (both depend only on `core:build`), with repeated `Blocking waiting for file lock on package cache`/`on build directory` — `cli:build` sat blocked until `crates-binding:build` released the lock. Total: 17.9s. CI's actual gate and `just ci`/`lint`/`test` were already safe — they call `cargo ... --workspace` directly, never through moon's per-project fan-out.

**Fix:**
- `justfile`'s `build` recipe: replaced `moon run :build` with `cargo build --workspace --exclude oxc-react-docgen-napi`, then `moon run napi:build vite-plugin:build` for the two TS-side steps that still need moon's dependency graph (no cargo lock involved there).
- `package.json`'s `build`/`test`/`lint`: same pattern — direct workspace-wide `cargo` invocations, with `test` also running vite-plugin's vitest suite directly via `pnpm --filter`.
- No affected-only fan-out bug existed to fix — CI's affected-detection is already coarse (whole Rust workspace or skip, never per-crate `-p`), so that part of the described fix pattern didn't apply here.

**Verified:** same clean-rebuild scenario after the fix — 11.9s, only a brief solo lock touch (not contention between two racing processes). `pnpm lint` (529... wait, that's test) clean clippy across both crates; `pnpm test` — 529 Rust tests + 33 vitest tests, all green. `just ci` now gets past `fmt`/`clippy` cleanly; it still fails on pre-existing markdown-format debt in 17 unrelated files (not something I introduced or am fixing here).

    args=()

**Publish order now accounts for dev-dependencies between same-batch packages**

- **Fixed:** `cargo publish` (run without `--no-verify`) rebuilds the packaged tarball to verify it, which needs every declared dependency -- including `[dev-dependencies]` -- resolvable from the registry. Publish ordering previously ignored dev-dependency edges entirely, so a package with a dev-dependency on a same-batch sibling could be published before that sibling, failing with an unresolvable version requirement.
- Dev-dependency ordering is best-effort, not a hard requirement: a legitimate mutual dev-dependency between two otherwise-unrelated packages no longer risks hard-failing the whole publish plan -- it falls back to the previous (non-dev) ordering for that case instead.

`moon run :build`/`:test`/`:lint`, which fans out one `cargo build/
clippy/nextest -p <crate>` per Rust crate. Every one of those processes

illusory — the crates serialized behind Cargo's own lock. Reproduced
live: `cli:build` sat blocked on `crates-binding:build`'s lock for the
full run (17.9s), with repeated "Blocking waiting for file lock" lines.

letting Cargo's own job scheduler parallelize compilation across crates
instead of moon's process-level fan-out. napi/vite-plugin still go
through moon — no Cargo lock involved there. Confirmed fix: same clean
rebuild, 11.9s, no contention. CI's own gate and `just ci`/`lint`/`test`
were never affected — they already called `cargo ... --workspace`
directly, bypassing moon's per-project tasks.
